quotes.text: I've told people that I feel more pain in a day than most people feel in a decade. But it's getting real. If you feel more pain in a decade than I feel in a bad ten minutes, then I pity you.
Brainrot: mine is a 56k modem in a broadband world.
Brainrot chapter on bucking up mistakes, making donors [?] the second thing, missing appointments.

Very not okay [?] — working on different sensory experiences and seeing what it does to the pain. Okay, granted this is not a valid test because I had a slug of cannabutter [?] and I'm not feeling much pain. I guess what I really want to say is I'd forgotten how much fun it is to throw a knife and stick it into an old stump. And I've got my knife from — what was it, third grade in Tallahassee, Florida — my beloved hunting knife and its sheath. It survived all these years of moves.
[unintelligible] — "very not just realized"

Brainrot: remember Ilmar Quisk [?] and his scale of consumer pleasure. Forget what it was called. There was a unit, though, and I joked about having a unit of pain, which we called the Agon. He worked at a corporate food producer's laboratory, research laboratory, and so they had labs where they would measure pleasurable responses. But we agreed that people — I remember the particular example. A particular example used was, you know, where on the Agon scale would be thrusting your face into a motorboat propeller.
Okay, it occurs to me that my 1 through 10 with emergency overrides to 25 scale is certainly a type of Agon scale. So maybe I should look up research metrics units.

Brainrot: last sentence of Crick's *What Mad Pursuit*, page 163. "It is essential to understand our brains in some detail if we are to assess correctly our place in this vast and complicated universe we see all around us."

Brainrot: making sure that I don't use my brainrot to avoid emotional issues. That was very important to me, especially in the marriage. I made it a rule that if a conversation — if I had to end an emotional conversation, that I would make a point of resuming the conversation when I felt better, so that my brainrot didn't become trained to be a way of avoiding discomfort.

Brainrot: gave myself a haircut. Just created me the buzz [?] and the switching between different depth combs and looking in the mirror — it's definitely fumbling. And this is the first time I had to cut down my hair significantly. The only other time I gave myself a haircut it was just growing in, but I got a clipper because I wanted to save the anguish of visiting a barber — even a quiet barber, which they are by nature not. And then talk about Myra.

Brainrot could be one of the first chapters. Oh, okay. My philosophy, or one of my philosophies, is: since life has definitely smacked me in the face with a lemon, I'm not going to settle for lemonade. I'm going to make lemon meringue pie, one of my favorite foods.
Brainrot. That's this style — my style in general. It's P.G. Wodehouse meets Kafka. And in Brainrot, that's seasoned with some Oliver Sacks and a dollop of Thoreau.
Brainrot includes some thanks from the covert comic [?].
Brainrot. A lot of my handicaps make it seem like I'm lazy or not trying. Losing things, being unable to clean up things, forgetting things.

The Brainrot vision of my body is maybe a Rube Goldberg machine, or just a stripped-down efficient description — robotic description of pain, receptors in nerves and thalamus. Trip-down description [?].

But in that, maybe a chapter shaped around the rhythm of the day — the freshness in the morning and pain level in the morning, events that can happen during the day, and the down, well, the upwelling of pain throughout the day.

Brainrot: the creation of the book — how Kate, you were instrumental in making it happen. Having taken voice notes for years, with my weaknesses in sorting and organizing in general, as I accumulated voice notes the prospective task of transcribing and organizing them became more and more intimidating and implausible.
Brainrot: marbled with pain, a juicy kind of knee [?].

This is weird, but I've got to watch my computer use. It does wear on me. And it's hard to be creative when your medium is painful to use — like a painter with a brush that's covered in shards of broken glass.

Just thinking about stimulus — you know, would wearing gloves add enough stimulus, like putting socks on? You know, I wear clothes. I'm getting some feedback from there, but maybe the hands. That'd be weird, if wearing gloves gave me enough input to short-circuit a lot of the pain. Oh well, this is an unexpected avenue.

Brainrot. Okay — *New Scientist*, July 16th through 22nd 2005, page 49, an article called "The Darkest Seduction," about depression. Topic of this little section: can depression inspire genius or creativity? I wonder if the notion that depression is linked to creativity is related to the idea that depression is a lot like passion. I think it is the opposite, and it involves very narrow, flattened emotions. It's true that very often extreme experience informs art and makes a tale interesting. That can go for cancer, or in the novelist John Updike's case, psoriasis. Diseases give people a strong individual perspective, but that truth is usually an argument against dealing with handicapping conditions. Perhaps the whole question is less interesting than it is made out to be.
Brainrot. I'm a connoisseur of very subtle differences in cognition and consciousness.

I need to get people to help adhere to structures, like I set up the wikis, and I still think that they may be the way to go, but I'd rather discover that they were inadequate for trying to use them, rather than just let them fall aside. I'm not talking about the Brainrot, but that is being used — I'm talking about what to do, and also talking about the help I'll need, setting up a daily schedule, which again keeps — I keep forgetting to do.
Brainrot: the freakishly smart thing — the ant in high heels IQ metaphor.

Tough. I am by the gate, and just realizing I depended on her more than I thought, and part of the reason the last year has been so scattered for me is that she was helping share me [?] and keep me on track and keep me thinking and discussing what I was doing. Now I don't have that, and because everything is painful it's like — I don't know, I'm trying to think of a metaphor where there's a plane of sandpaper and something like a little pea or a cube of sugar, whatever, and it gets stuck. It's a little push to get just — it's just the sticking friction or whatever it's called, but it's more than that because it is painful. I know it's going to be painful and I'm going to be exhausted afterwards, but I can do things. I don't get the automatic confusion and I can push through. I should talk to Kellen about this and of course, mainly Brooke. I do need to code on a much more micro scale, because I've relaxed as much as I can, because now I've got that — well, I'm tiring myself out just doing mundane chores, because I can. Such as rewiring the stereo, which I was absolutely shaking and hand-jerking, and oh, it took a lot, but I pushed through it. It took five, eight times as long as it would have back in the day, but I kept pushing and I did it. And then I did the drug stack and vacuuming, and that was — that was the day I talked to Kate. So I pushed myself, but I had woken up that morning resolved to get through my whole to-do list, and I got three things done, which was amazing. I mean, one of them was really hard though, the rewiring. I was just like, okay, I don't know — wheelchair racers, your bungee cord or something. I picked the activity most likely to antagonize the disability, but I did it. But that wore me out. The pain threw me a whole [?] — I went into a freewheeling non-sleep schedule because of the pain, dull it with the vaporizer and just be drifting off when it would start biting again. I probably should explore eating again for the high pain days. So I guess I drifted down to around — maybe try to be accurate with pain scales, but I was thinking it was less than 50% of the, you know, four-year-old pain, but it's now more than that. It's, I don't know, six or whatever. But that sucks. That cannot be reiterated. It's sufficient.
Be sure and talk to Brooke about needing a coach, a fine-grained manager.

Just thinking about the nature of this, the pain, and why — now that I have the luxury of time — it's hard for me to do things, and everything I do, especially complex things, will exact a toll. It will be from very painful to words [?] I care to invent. I lose that thought. Listen. And...

Okay, extending the last observation: now that I have the luxury of time, it's hard for me to do anything because it's going to be painful. Why it's easy for something as simple as my mouth guard lying there by the coffee maker maybe three weeks. So anywho, it's like — well, I feel like I have comment [?]. It's just been war in choosing a task, pulling the trigger, doing it. It's like going on a mission or starting a considerable effort, a marathon, a pain marathon. The other night, rewiring the back of the center, which was a horrific rat's nest of cables and dust that I was unable to contemplate for years, but put on the to-do list as a high priority because I knew I could do it now that I don't automatically get confusion. It was a horrible day. I wished myself, jokingly — I'm going to hold [?] the items on my to-do list, knowing that a laughable ambition, but gallant. The wiring right away, and it was like, okay, charge. It's not like "okay, time to do this thing," it was like up the ladders and out of the trenches. Gritting teeth and shaking and taking long breaks and taking four hours where it would have taken 45 minutes. But cleaning it up, dusting the inside of that cabinet, labeling the end of each cord. And I even stopped halfway through doing the rewiring when I realized that there was a more elegant solution. But I'd have to backtrack a bit, you know. Sometimes you have to eat pain to do the right thing. And now at this point there are some tasks I can decide to do arbitrarily well, I guess, if you speak [?]. But the lesson, the bitter lesson: that if something needs to be done, if something's worth doing, that's worth doing poorly. I guess if you look at it strictly from a survival point of view, which I've been forced to, it's obvious. One thing — you need to bring the wood in, while doing it well would entail cleaning up the mess neatly, the snow, and the boots. But if you need to have the wood in, and just the wood in is going to bust a couple of rivets in the boiler anyway, forget about doing it well. Just do it. Do it poorly, but do it. So the whole point of rewiring the back of the DVD and the monitor and the Xbox and the VCR, and the aquarium pumps and lights and a few other plugs in that area, and wiring through the wall from the computer studio to the player, was to make a really nice — not a nightmare. I rarely need to look back there, but to make it not a nightmare, to make it something I could be proud of. And so because now I can push and just experience pain without automatically getting confused at high levels of pain, I was able to do a really good job and I was able to backtrack when I made a mistake. Or it wasn't a mistake, it was just an inelegance — a solution that I saw and rectified with acceptable costs and Agons. So I need a coach: cheer me on, to track day-to-day. Details in time are just not my strong suits, and especially when they're mixed together. And so I'm going to ask Brooke to be my day-to-day coach and help me set goals and achieve them, and to clearly identify patterns in productivity, to help me enforce relaxation — weekends. Maybe that's weekends. And just set a number of goals and keep daily touch and discuss and brainstorm, and have to justify not doing stuff or doing stuff that I hadn't planned on doing. Analyzing my time, try timed activity, schedule — semi-rigid to rigid schedule might just be the perfect thing for me, frankly, now that I think of it, with some sort of resting mechanism. So I wasn't feeling constantly guilty of blowing my schedule. That would not be a life optimization. So anyway, that feels good, and yeah, so that is the decision.
Brainrot: hot sand and grit mixed in the muscles.

I just think about the old — and the much-nest spear-in-the-chest pains [?] — and just how it felt like I'd grown a whole nother bouquet of nerve endings that just thrust upward from my chest, so the hot electric spears could pierce down through the nerves and ghost meat and jelly, gray jelly hung with the flamed nerves pumping pure agony straight to the...

It's like they stuck three or four electrified pencils into the front of my feet, and some hand is jerking them slowly around and twisting them and spreading them and crunching them together — and this sort of oozy, clenching, abrasive, hot.
Brainrot: the Hetrix [?] story there — as I had my mind clear and free, but it wasn't to be.

Like standing in a thistle field naked [?], or if you stand real still in a special way only a few thistle flowers are having it. It's not very inviting to go anywhere, and you know you're deriving satisfaction from describing my home [?].
Oh man, I was just dictating into the mouthpiece of the volcano bag. A fairly good idea.

Yeah, synesthesia and pain. Really the best flavor descriptor for the pain is bitter, sometimes metallic. Sometimes when it's puke-your-brains-out time there is actually a regurgitant undertone to the taste.
Sometimes the pain — sometimes the pain isn't subtle or obscure. It's just raw fucking pulse.

Just thinking about my — the feeling that I have that the area of my brain that writes and programs is rested now, and I can use it, but that it's fragile. And it's like I want to guard it and just husband it. It's rested and able, but it's not robust. I can easily overdo it. Just thinking of it in terms of game and healing RPG stats — it's like some sort of a break or something like that, unfortunately, and that it's rare now. But some sort of stat healer, and long-range stat healing that initiates a release of talents.
Brainrot: I've regressed to one of those "one, two, many" counting cultures.

Sorting through boxes of old papers, and I've got a box of printouts of email to CI Host around 2000, 2001, and it looked like they were dunning me for 900 bucks and I have completely forgotten it. But it's interesting looking at these printouts — I was printing out things over and over, very characteristic behavior, just not getting it. Remember being angry at CI Host? I'm not reading the correspondence. I'm not interested in anger archaeology. A lot of printouts of email to them, forum threads, and bills, so...

I've got tons of printouts of stuff about CI Host. I've just gone through a box, thrown stuff away, and had about a ream of printouts of Slashdot articles and correspondence, bills. I can remember being angry — they were in trouble and tried to nick me for like 900 bucks. And then tons of stuff about epilepsy and medical marijuana, about another ream of paper that I never even glanced at after I printed it out.
I'd rather be nice than smart, if I had to.

"Nice" is a word that becomes odd after very few repetitions. Just thinking that "nice" is often used as a put-down — "oh, real nice" — and kids' mom used it as the ultimate sarcastic stiletto. But I'd be quite happy if someone described me as a nice guy.
"Nice" again, just triggered by the fact that I use the word a lot as a comment in written-in-blood critiques, and that it's not sarcastic.
Do the Hetrix [?] story as a blog entry, as a draft.
Love talking to people. I love being in a room full of people smarter than I am talking about some crazy —

For Brainrot: running a metaphor into the gridiron. Just go like crazy with a football metaphor — the infinitely long football field. Getting up every morning on the field, looking down the field, and okay. It's just — I just got too stacked up, kind of boxed in [?]. Lateral to myself.
Maybe my life is like doing a reduced-palette painting, or working in a restricted metric form.
Talk about reading *Frontline* [?], or talk about some other books' passages — keeping-it-in-perspective chapter.
I am fueled by fire.

Okay. Catch up with voice notes daily. It's dysfunctional when they pile up. Yeah, it's something that I should do before talking to Brooke every day, and we should put that on a checklist. And I think — talk to Brooke tonight about having a daily checklist, and that would be "up to date on voice notes," because that, yeah.
Okay, sunset is now going to be the time for the dogs, and music, and good smell, and... I was just talking to — did some good things then. So...
Okay, it's sunset day. Yeah, this is really good. Sunset, every day. With the dogs, looking at the sunset, listening to "Gonna Curly-O" [?].

Just on the coaching level, thinking in terms of setting goals right now, and how setting the end of April was a fun and a positive thing, but I don't want to get hung up on it. And how in the past, free-writes and writes, I've been very overt about tracking my progress and predicting finishing things like that — but I was weller then. And I have to — one of the difficulties is I have to learn different lessons depending on different levels of wellness. What worked in the last year certainly doesn't work now, and so you've got to learn those lessons.
I was thinking about software that would help me in my rewrite, and then I realized — interposing software between me and finishing Hel's Bet: poor choice.

Thinking about today's rewriting with red pencil of Hel's Bet, and that it was getting pretty static-y there in the second hour, and that I need to be aware of that. And this is crucial for the game too: that my enthusiasm, joy of work — enthusiasm for ideas and joy of work — can cause me to...

I've just noticed that I'm about to skip transcribing voice notes for the second day. It started out, I don't want to transcribe right before I do my big writing push. I'll wait a while — and then of course it was up to show [?].
Make the Brainrot notes into a story.
Brainrot notes: a story called "Betty's Inferno."
Sometimes I feel like every day is like a series of 440s. You know, your dash — it's just painful effort after painful effort.

I'm going to make a note of that on my voice recorder. I did transcribe all ten from yesterday. So tomorrow I want to talk to you about fine-grain dealing with distractions and obsessive thoughts. Just think about it and just describe it to you and bounce some ideas back and forth. So I've been trying distraction and just various things. I mean, I was hoping that the canoe trip would get my mind off, but it wasn't real successful. But all day, even though I was sputtering around in the morning, I've had a real confidence that I'm going to have a good slugger [?] writing tonight, and so anyway I guess right now that's what I want to do. Yeah, right, right, yeah — and it feels good and I think I'm going to have a couple prime hours. And so anyway, so talk tomorrow. I'm going to get up at 9 and get in to do the licensing tomorrow. Yeah, you know, right, whatever — and then I'll see, I may go into the cities and do that. Aaron [?], but what's your evening like tomorrow night? Yeah. How about if I pick up something for dinner — and for sure, I mean, well, check with your lovely wife and if that's cool, I'll come and do some talking and just — great. Okay, cool. Cool. Well, you name it. Yeah. Well, it's 6:30. How about 6:30? Okay. So, how's your other — what, oh, I'm not going to talk a lot, we'll talk tomorrow. I want to hear about what else, other things you're up to. And so, okay, well, cool. And I'm feeling hopeful about this, so. And I did my sit-ups first thing this morning, that's the best way to do it. And it's so funny because the dogs are impatient for their meat and Travis starts barking. But okay, talk tomorrow.
Dramaton: the interpreter — on the commands, the non-flow-control commands should pass the command as the command in the execute-command parameters. Oh, I think it actually does that.

I can't show my strength through brute force. When I push, I'll show my strength through persistence. By not giving up, again and again — not the force of the raging river, but of the slow drip. My strength is not the force of a raging river. It's just a slow drip in an underground cave building a stalactite, molecule by molecule.

One of the kinships I feel with AI experimenters and theorists is due to my brainrot and the way that I've watched various semi-discrete processing centers in my brain degrade. It tends to foster a — well, and of course I've been really analytical about my own skills. Very aware of the various degradations. So it fosters a sense of communion with those that are trying to build synthetically what I have been living with and analyzing.

Brainrot coaching. Just thinking about my problems with keeping track of figures. Like today I was going to — I had some expenses, but they're just minor things: a pet shop, whatever, yard supplies, gas. And so I thought, oh, I'll just tell Brooke I'm having dinner with him tonight, and all the numbers just flew out of my brain, inaccessible. I wrote a check to renew my license. I honestly can't tell you if it's 39 or 49 or 69, they all — but at the time, I had it [?] writing it down because it was just so easy, it's always just silly. So I know my memory is bad, but I underestimate how bad, because I'm still not used to it. Even when I'm thinking "should I write this down," my thought is, oh yeah, I have a really bad memory and probably should write it down — and then, oh no, this is trivial, save writing numbers down for when you have two numbers or something hot [?]. But because at three different times today I had a little number I thought I'd remember, and it just completely interfered, overwrote, whatever, with one another.

Just — I don't know why this hit me, but just thinking about Mom, and the fact of their tough years of her alcoholism, but how they made that into something pretty amazing and improved their marriage. So just a model of going through just hellish times, but not letting go. That is huge.

Brainrot and coaching. What I see in my mind more and more is that shell-shocked little animal — well, electric-shocked. The shocked animal, the dazed animal punished for touching anything. And I've got to drag this thing through my difficult areas by whatever means necessary, and that means going through —
And sometimes I have to overbelieve in myself, because it's how I could do anything.

Ah, Brainrot. Thank goodness that Brooke is coming Friday. I went to just put away a couple of the boxes that are stacked up around the house after emptying the storage. And... oh, did I get sick quick. Oh yeah. Chest pains — the closest I've been to a seizure in many months.
How, you know, neuroplastic exercises are talking about practice and burning in, creating new neural associations through repetitive exercise. Now it's practice. Practice makes permanent.
And sometimes, being tortured so cruelly and incessantly, I doubt the fundamental benevolence of the universe.
The neuroplastic model is attractive in that it returns agency. It accepts responsibility. It doesn't just wait for mysterious things to change. So I think in terms of Brainrot, this is —
Brainrot: Keppra affects performance. You know, the little man in your head that lights off the orgasm rocket when he gets excited — Keppra makes him very sleepy.

Note to Brooke [?]: help me with the model. What are we talking about? And then use computer metaphors — there's patching, there's overriding, erasing. This search is at the neuro level, for me to read [?].
And it's Randall [?] for further reading on neuroplasticity.

Holistic. They're talking about, Brainrot, the overall health-level concept — that is, you know, I never really thought it through. What is it? Some sort of summation? The state of all my various subsystems? Or is there a health meter hovering over my head I'm not aware of?

Yeah, I really do feel like I'm on a writing retreat, and I'm going to cultivate that feeling and write it for all it's worth. Because the last months it's been confronting my pain and weakness daily — just running into the brown bulls [?] daily, inching through the field of thistles. And the painful part is now fun, because I'm doing it with Brooke. The assembling of the parts that I want to work with in a chapter is now much simpler, because I'm storytelling out loud, and acting, and Brooke is recording. And just the value to me of not having to switch states is immense, is critical.

I have not admitted to myself how painful the rewrite process has been. I'm a connoisseur of pain in an involuntary rather than whatever decadent sense. The quality of the pain that I experience when I'm grappling with the elements of writing is — what's the right word — esoteric, ethereal, very subtle. But the main pain, the result of the pain, is devastating to my progress in the book, because it disrupts my thought processes. I mean, if you're thinking along and having a jolly little inspiration — I think a beaver is getting out of the lake and Travis is giving chase — if you're having a jolly little inspiration, somebody shoving a nice ice pick into your skull is a wee bit distracting. Even if somebody was sitting there and just pounding you with a feather, it would tend to break your train of thought. So having little sparklers of pain, even though on the Agon scale they're registering in the .05 range — you don't need the heavy artillery of agony to disrupt delicate thought processes. Last clause to be reworded.

I'm having some insights as I talk, and that's helpful. But — okay, where was I? There. Who knows? Well, my insight, my inspiration was to ask Brooke to help me even more, to get into the trenches in the book and to help me create a task list for me, for each chapter, that he and I would talk through — and that I would separate the writing from the thinking through the plot, which paragraph goes there, into very specific task lists. And as soon as I thought of it, and when he said "I'll do whatever it takes to get it out the door," I just relaxed, because suddenly — this is exactly what I needed. And so I had the first session today and I haven't had so much fun in forever, because it freed me. It was so liberating, because he was being secretary and I was acting out the scene and describing these characters — and he's getting up to speed still in the book, but we're only on the 7th chapter out of 80, so there was very little to fill him in on. And so my normal routine when I write scenes is I act them out internally and I do the facial expressions and things like that. It's really improv. And I'll go over and over and just cherry-pick the best thing. So I was up on my feet acting things out, and he was taking down notes. And so we've got the things that I got from the rewrite, which is I'll bring in character development, I need more on this motivation and things like that. I've got great notes. And so after he's got some notes out, then we go back through my summation of the — and it's fun, because it's like a puzzle rather than impossible, which it was. It was just that I have brain damage and that capability has gone from me. And I just love and miss collaboration, and this is — I mean, this is Brooke, you have to drag words out of him, but they're always very good. I mean, they're always right on, and I just really value his input. So he got it right away. It actually became — in practice it was more fun than I had imagined, because I hadn't really envisioned that it was me acting through the scenes, making it up, and Brooke jotting down notes. I thought we'd be talking and discussing, but my natural thing is to act it out and make sure it sounds right and feels right. And Brooke's getting it. He's so funny because he's just like Buster Keaton — I mean he's stone-faced. I'm not used to working creatively with a person like that. There's occasional misunderstanding, like if I switch to another persona and all of a sudden that person doesn't know things. I mean, you know, the theatrical stuff. He doesn't know the name of somebody and I'm doing so — he said, "but that's Chin," I said, okay, but he doesn't know that, he's the runt. And I can tell Brooke's digging it. I'm just like, okay, he understood, I have all the parts and they're ready to go. And I said, of course, this whole book I've had a movie in mind, and the scene that we went through is a really fun one with reversals, where you have some danger and it gets resolved and they're celebrating and then you hit them with something three times worse. So it was illuminating for him to watch that. And for me — a lot of this stuff is from a lot of my awareness, and the improvements come directly from the writing group and the critiques. They're just gold. Oh, it was inspiring and painful. It just put me in an impossible situation which I kept trying to wiggle through and around. My unfortunate metaphor was that I'm standing naked in a field of thistles and I've got to walk through a hundred yards of them to get to my goal — and when you do that, any shiny little rock along the way is going to look really attractive, to just stand and look at it and not move forward and take the thistles. So anyway, it just transformed what I — I felt constantly under the gun, just with an impossible test that shouldn't be impossible, because I'd done it before. And that added to the frustration. And all I could say was, I'm slowly moving forward, but it was not very satisfying — in the sense that I was always grateful to be able to write when I had so many years when I couldn't write a sentence. And so I always tried to keep it in perspective. So I just said, I'm on a writing retreat, I'm on a vacation, and I would have anyway. We went down to the dock with the dogs. I just sat and they had fun and it's just so beautiful there. I was just able to enjoy it so much more because I know that this is going to be published, and I've wanted that all my life. It's really motivating when people I respect are enthusiastic. At the end of our session today, I could see it clicked in Brooke's mind that this is — he's always had faith in me and respected me, but I think that that session sort of brought it home. I could see that scene up on the screen. That was sweet. It was like a switch went on in him: okay, we're going to get this out the door. Then of course he is going to be helping me circulate and promote it. So he's so funny about money and things like that, but I'm getting him 5% now just to help me get it out the door, any money I receive, and just gladly. I'm not trying to cash in on this. If you're cashing in on 5%, I'm going to be floating on cash — so you know how happy that would make me, for you to get money. And he's also got 5% of Channel Zilch, which is Margaret and my — it's just, he has 5, Kellen has 5, and then Margaret and I each have 45. So honestly, with her space explorer, I could just goof off and she's going to make money. People like it. So anyway — oh man, painful, but inch by inch, and with Brooke's hand, it opens a door forward for me beyond this project. And because it seems real, the money pressure isn't as great. I mean we're still like, really, really — Brooke does my budgets and I get my allowance and that just works out great. Just trying to work around my weaknesses, and this will do it. Yeah. So, oh, it's going to be fun. And I still have one painful task, but I do it in the morning, and that's every day. But I made it less painful. I'm always tinkering with my lifestyle. Another thing I recently realized was I was letting my voice notes build up because it's painful for me to transcribe and sort them. And so I would just have like five, you know, 500 voice notes, literally, and that meant to me three days of pain and a couple days of recovery. And so now I just make it a rule to always stay current. And so — huh, yeah, it's transformative. It's just like now I can get to work and just do what I do best, and the book's going to be better. Well, I'm thinking sometime mid to late May, on a really sort of fun — and the nice thing is I'll be able to, well, with my patrons it doesn't really matter. Playing scales — but as long as it's in tune, it's hard to make a harp sound bad. As long as it doesn't have pedals on it, which mine doesn't. Okay, well, that would make a nice little bicycle, a harp steering mechanism. Cut your fingertips off while you play, Jane [?]. Visceral rhythm.

It's my tinkering with the minutiae of my lifestyle to maximize profit. I lost the train of thought. Seeing some deer out in the field — I was walking to the mailbox and I got distracted by three deer laying down in the field in the distance.

Okay — it's not so much the minutiae. By trying to change my fundamental lifestyle — it's not the right word, but always jockeying to discover and practice techniques that work for me. I'm always battling the force of habit. Habits are generally a really good thing; without habits we'd be thinking — we'd have been operating at a very low level. Some habits — in implementing new habits, specifically not letting the — staying ahead of the pain. Just a frog with boiling water. Somehow the water was on the inside instead of the outside. But they just made a habit of ignoring it until it was — [unintelligible]. And so, my awareness. I talked about my priorities on the tactical decision. It's not that bad.
So I ran to do [?] a one- or two-page comic about my brainrot.

Brainrot. The bubbles — as I talk, in pain sometimes it feels like glassy, waxy bubbles shattering in my mouth as I talk, breaking, and shards. That's a bit of a sparkling feeling, but with clear — like every syllable, I think, syllable. Maybe the sensation has to do with trying to map the proprioceptive feedback from mouth positioning as pain. And so — what in speech does a tongue snap between positions and sustain sounds? Does it position the tongue very smoothly? Do we see the tongue popping from position to position as you talk? Or if you slowed it down, would it move languidly rather than pop and snap? The shattering seems to be on a syllabic basis, and it's the shards — I don't feel them, let's say. I just feel the snapping, and for an instant, a little of a crunch. They don't — broken glass doesn't accumulate. I just feel a shard for a second. It's like mouthfuls of Christmas tree ornaments, you know — every syllable, a glass Christmas tree ornament shattered in my mouth, and then somebody immediately puts in a new one to shatter on the next syllable. And the sensation is very — it's muscle-bound, it has to do with tongue position. It leads to me the sort of, I don't know — how am I speaking that way now? No, I'm not in a great deal of pain right now. I'm stoned. That's loquacious. But in pain, when talking, I often get high, monotone, arcing words out, spitting them out. And part of it is that unpleasant sensation of glass — a just continuous sparkle and pain and shard and cut, every single one.
Intelligent design and central pain syndrome. Brainrot.
Recovering from brainrot, recovering from being a beat-up little animal. I'm just trying to feel [?] trouble in the world.

A metaphor is — I regret having to, but they just felt like these electric worms just sort of writhing their way up my legs through the bottom of my feet, and just sort of slowly wiggling. Sort of like a taffy machine. They're sort of like gummy worms in the field, in that they're at that size and they have the ridges that are sort of rippling through my muscles. And just a really unnecessary metaphor that I'm driven to construct. Let me see, they're not hot, they're not sharp, which is a blessing, but they're really, really electric. Just like little electric worms, just writhing up my legs. And not really paying — well, you know, I don't like focusing on the pain, micro-focusing and trying to get more fine-grained with my — I guess my trying to focus. It's not proprioceptive, it's just, you know, what are you doing selectively focusing on a small [part] of any incoming sense? So the point being, after that [unintelligible] flavored and not immediately recollectable construct that I — you know, mid-sentence, I was, as I was cobbling together the metaphor of the electric worms, I was beginning to like feel whether, or trying to evaluate the incoming sense data, to see if it felt like the worms were avoiding my bones. I had an image of them crawling up my veins through my muscles, but as more of a gross description of the feeling. So just as, you know, you the reader, if you're whole, can through the power of sensorial filtering or whatever suddenly query your left pinky finger to say, how's it feeling, bud? And, you know, hey, really dive into it — is it warm, relaxed, is it touching something rough, slick? And as you focus your whatever sensorial awareness budget into your pinky, the rest of your awareness of the rest of your body fades, attenuates, whatever the word is. Same phenom. And a part of what I'm doing, along with vaporizing, is recoiling from the fine-grain focus on the phantom neuropathic pain to describing it. It's like any words that describe this pain — or are you [distanced] from this because there are no words bad enough [for the] experience? So despite my own described nature of language, [it] makes it impossible to convey experience. Which is a good thing. It would be a horrible, horrible power to embed in language, to convey pain in less than euphemistic [terms] — like [women] forgetting the pain of childbirth, an evolutionary advantage given that if they remembered, one child would be the maximum anyone would have. So too would the — so too, although in a negative sense, it would never advantageously evolve, the ability to convey pain through language. Well, it might be an advantage to an individual who possessed the power. I guess part of it is just a question of mechanics. It's a rather large chunk to evolve willy-nilly. But the organism would have to evolve to receive the pain, perhaps. Unless the words could directly manipulate the nerves in the hearer to evoke identical sensation, which —

I'm trying to take a break from the MJ. I've gone 48 hours, but I'm not gonna — maybe, well, I'm, let's see, probably gonna decide later when I'm in bed. I'm going to get to sleep, or read. Anyhow, I'm disappointed. I made it five days in the spring, but nothing else does my pain any good. Current, with my medication, that hasn't gone [far enough] to get through the night without...

quotes.text: Just trying to... That sounds like something that you wouldn't like me to do. Yeah. Don't do what I'm doing. Do something different. Don't get my slits[?] every day. Give me the camera. I'll get some pictures of you guys. Oh, don't bother looking pretty, I just take random jacks[?]. And don't knock on the ice too near a dam, Marty. There's a stretch in the bike trail going that — come on up on this fish set here.

Okay, here's what I got out of the [session], an insight that practice — okay, to monitor the trigger. To monitor my pain level; don't let it get above a certain point, because I'm practicing pain. I'm practicing feeling lousy.

...procedure. Did I ever even try it? Oh, yeah. Well, I like to say it. So, for example, right now I would put my pain [level] at about a 2 out of 10, which given my activity last week is good. Things have been coming together, various parts of my life, but I am very encouraged by the neuroplastic techniques that Dr. Brendel suggested that I pursue. And so I want to nail down and specify and understand that better. And he had recommended that I use a smell that is very relaxing to me, and so I started just doing regular periods where I would smell a balsam pillow. But I discovered — essentially we were trying to practice feeling well — and I found that tactile pleasure of petting my dogs was much more powerful than the smell. Okay, kind of doing some experimenting there. Oh, very much so. And so I was combining various, you know, like, at sunset on a cabin overlooking a zillion-dollar view of the sunset or evening, you know, put on some melt-your-mind-heart music and sit with my dog and my pillow. And really powerful sensations that I haven't felt in a long while, of like pain completely flickering out. And so I switched — well, I realized that I was doing a lot of things where I just accept, you know, pain, because I just had it for years and I just sort of gritted my teeth and ignored it. And that I decided, rather than just doing periodic sessions, I would try to recognize when my pain was at its greatest and then spend some quality time with the [dogs and the] good smells. And that is really powerful. — And effective, huh? — Yeah. — Okay, good. Yeah, I'm glad. Now, you said you're about a two today, as far as being a one? — And it'll go, you know, it's up to three or four right now. But that always happens when I talk. — All right. Now, with everything in consideration here, you're doing all this, like, tactile stimulation and olfactory stimulation there. So at the worst, how bad does the pain get with you practicing all these things and putting your mind in a different place? — Well, there's during the session, you know. Right now I'm pretty much doing every sunset and then as needed. And my upper level of pain — overall my pain levels have been down, you know. I mean, I haven't seen a 10 for a long time. — For a long time? — No. — That is great. — No. — Great. When the pain does come along, where is it physically located? — It's, you know, it's neuropathic pain. I was diagnosed — I have a seizure disorder that was out of control for a number of years, and the pain was, you know, secondary after that. — After the seizure disorder? — Yeah. So the pain is somewhat classically the diabetic neuropathic leg pain. And as it progresses — I mean, the very first time actually I had a seizure that was detected, it exhibited a heart-attack-like pain shooting down my arm. That's very rare, but I felt some of it recently, mainly because I've increased my activity level because of lack of pain. I'm finishing a novel, and it's... — Sometimes it's hard to do when you're hurting, trying to keep it focused. — Because, well, I have problems with complexity as a result of my seizures. I was a programmer at Microsoft, I lost a lot. And so I have an aide who — we're even working more closely now, getting this rewrite done, and that's my main focus, and he's also my coach, and I check in every day on my pain levels and discuss strategies for, yeah, roadblocks I've run into. And so I've just had a ton of fun bringing him on board the book, because he hadn't read it up to this week and I've been working on it forever. And I'm in this writing group, and two of the eight of us have gotten book deals in the last six months, so it's really, really exciting. — Yeah, yeah. — And so the focus is, you know, me finishing this, which is about a month or six weeks away, and not burning out. Because I've had project after project over the last couple years that I've just overdone it and burnt out. So we're doing really well, and I'm having more fun than I've had in a long time. — Good. — Because I really like collaborating and being with people, but, you know, it's hard. — Tell me, you've been well as far as medically and surgically, you haven't had the flu or the cold or anything? — Yeah, it's been well now. — Okay. Seizure-wise, have you had any? — My seizures have been under good control. I've been in my cabin for five years and I had a great neuropsychiatrist who finally got them under control before I came out here. So in the last five years I've only had, I would say, two seizures, and the last one was about three years ago. But honestly, in the last month I did have — or I did come closer than I have for a long while, mainly because of my increased interaction and activity — and it didn't scare me. I mean, I don't have grand mals, so, you know, my life would be a lot different, I wouldn't be driving and things like that. And I just have tons of warning, so, you know, it wasn't scary, but it was just an indication that I had to look [out]. Yeah, and I mean, I'm super blessed. I'm on social security disability and I have some — you know, I'm really blessed, I've got some wealthy friends in the game industry who are backing me financially. So it's really — I'm very interested in this book in about six weeks to a month. Oh yeah, it's going to — it's a science fiction book called Hel's Bet. That's H-E-L apostrophe S, and Hel's — the Halloween's kid[?] is the protagonist. Helsbet.com, if you want to see it. — Okay, I'm going to write it down: H-E-L. — S-B-E-T dot com. — B-E-T dot com. I know, is there something out there now that you know is a lead-up? — Oh, all I have is an image from the book that a friend did years ago, yeah. — Well, I'm interested here. — Oh, it's going to — I'm very confident it's going to get published. — Oh, I bet so. — So, it's exciting. — You'll be seeing your picture on the back of the book, so, right? Is that how it works? — I wanted that my whole life, so, yeah. — All right, well, that's a good goal. That's a good goal to have. — That's what it is. — Frank, you'll be in shortly. — Okay, thanks. Various things are coming together, but really hopeful about [neuro]plastic techniques to overcome it. I've had some very powerful results so far just sort of fumbling and trying different things. So I just realized, you know, I'll get scatterbrained as we talk. But, you know, I want to get you up to date on what's happening and what I've tried and what's worked. And I'd like to have a model in my mind for what sort of neuroplastic changes might be occurring, because it's easy to visualize, you know, something spreading from one center to — you know, something to occupy more space. And I know it would just be all making stuff up, but just some thoughts. I want to try to systematize searching for the most powerful things. And I think by presenting what I've tried so far, you'll have some ideas for me to try. And then I'm in the last stages of rewriting the novel, and I'm feeling very optimistic about it getting published. After that, which has been a big effort, I want to get a tip-to-toe reevaluation of my condition. It's been a couple of years with Dr. Webster, if that's right. But reading your literature, you're not interested [in] just fix[ing] one little part. So I really want to work with you in a group. And, you know, further references to read. I reread the Doidge[?] book, and I've met three times with Bruce Youngberg, and he's read most of the book. He gave it back to me at the last session because we actually had — he wanted me to read some stuff. So that was very good. And he's — I've been discussing it as I've tried various things. — He's used some tactics like that on another guy we have coming up here that we're working with, to try to put himself in a mindset so we can get through a procedure without a catastrophe, at least an emotional catastrophe. And, you know, there's two parts to things. There's the actual treatment, which is kind of physical, and then there's the mental health perception of the treatment as well as how it goes. So this guy, unfortunately, didn't do well with the mental health part of just starting the procedure. So we're working on some things, the same ideas. So really, what I gathered from talking to those folks is, it's like, if I wanted to get this muscle big, I couldn't just go do something a couple times and have it big. You know, it takes a long time to reroute and to imprint something. — Yeah. — Negative or positive, luckily. You know, if you have one negative event that's visual, like when you see your child drown, that's stuck in there. How does that get stuck in there forever, but yet other things we see every day we might never remember again? So we're trying to utilize that powerful pathway, which quite honestly I don't think anybody understands fully. But how that happens — we're trying to imprint a very positive emotion to override something that maybe is a physical issue. — Yeah. — So that's the game we're playing with our brain, really. — Oh yeah, I mean, I call it practicing feeling good. And that's all — I mean, as soon as I started, you know, it's practice. And my daughter had a great piano teacher who said, no, practice doesn't make perfect. Practice makes permanent. So if you're practicing it the wrong way, that's the way you go. — That's actually a very good saying. — It is. — Practice makes permanent. — Yeah, and so — — I like that one. — Yeah, well, it's not copyrighted, so. — You should copyright it. So just to tell you about what I've gone through and what I've found effective, you know, I start and I'm actually — it's a serious amount of time. The smell of it is very rapid, you know. It's a lot of people —

Brain rot. So, I don't know if today's a furlough — it'd be a hell of a dirty trick. Best day I've had in maybe eight years. And I already — feeling warmth and amazing sensitivity to touch. Just touching and rubbing the dog is a lot more complex and sort of warm and soothing. I got out of the car after I went and bought pink things. And I could smell — it was not a good smell, the mailbox by the field, and they'd put down manure in the wind, or fall — and it felt nice. And the trees and the feel of the wind on my skin were all more vivid than they'd been for, I don't know, how long. And I'm going to have to adjust enough that pain is worse — yeah, because of the sensitivity, or not having any marijuana. But the one thing I dread is waking up with the same brain I had two days ago, a week ago. Today I actually considered jogging.

I just had a feeling like a giant thumb strummed across my thigh muscles, just sort of strumming them. Well, I'm really breaking in this new digital voice recorder. And, you know, normally it's like, okay, I'm camping, who cares if there's dirt in the bed, it's all character. And suddenly I'm like the princess and the pea. Okay, this is hypothesis: the pain down the foot is misinterpreted by the thalamus as pain — and perhaps a scientifically testable hypothesis — in me, in a way, the signal that is interpreted as pain is *no* sensation, you know, the bare skin in the air, whatever the standardized sensation of skin is. And so it needs a real signal, and that somehow damps it down. And, you know, the writhing — now I'm tired, I've stopped it, you know, cue the harp. And so the writhing is essentially trying to snuggle into the sheet, which is gritty. And the grit feels like a little — not shards of glass, but glass grit. But still, you know, it needs a sensation. The sheet I have on top of my legs does not provide enough pressure. And you know, I can probably think my way to a better solution than lying here feeling so much more than miserable.

Okay, well, this may be a — you know, okay, let's keep the — charging the machine guns and terror. quotes.text: It was in the year 1232 that Gregory established the Inquisition. In his bull, he declared that all heretics should suffer excommunication. Those who were condemned should not suffer their punishment at the hands of the Church but be handed over to the secular arm that sentence might be given and carried out by that body. The punishment for the unrepentant was burning at the stake, and even those who, having been found guilty of heresy, wished to repent, must suffer punishment, though not that of death. They should be condemned to perpetual imprisonment. All those who helped heretics in any way should suffer excommunication, and any who showed friendship for the excommunicated should themselves suffer excommunication. Those who were in such circumstances excommunicated would be given one year in which to prove they were not tainted with heresy. If they failed to do this, then they would fall into the hands of the Inquisition. Anyone discovered giving an excommunicated person Christian burial should immediately be excommunicated, and he should suffer under the ban until he took the offending corpse from its place of burial and arranged that ever after no one of the faith should be buried therein. Any persons, knowing that heresy existed, were bound in duty to the Church to inform on this. Failing to do so, they would incur excommunication and suspicion of being themselves involved in heresy. I really sort of anaesthetized myself to the suffering and horror. I was outraged to the maximum that I was capable of being outraged, and so I didn't need any more of that. At times I felt callous, because I was trying to suggest ideas that actually seemed to have made people act — well, they did. And at times I wondered if, by thinking on the tactical plane, I was not fully thinking out the repercussions on very vulnerable people. And yet I think my true hope was to plant a powerful, strong visual image that Bush is our employee, that we have the power to request him to resign. That power resides in our hands without wrinkling the Constitution in the least. And so I felt that I could afford to be a bit callous, cold — it's all thinking like a game player. I was not kidding when I said "checkmate in 10 days", because anybody that saw that would know how I was thinking. And I think everybody was in shock and horror and appalled at the dereliction and callousness — and three more years of this bumbling idiot at the controls of the most powerful nation that ever lived. Come on, what's to be hopeful about? And so, this bit of political theatre — remind people that Bush works for us, that we would not let his behaviour pass by in anybody who we employed. Purely horrible business sense. In the next couple days I want to extend that vision to suggest healing and hope. My idea that I call civil disobedience siege ergonomics — thinking about that 80-year-old Republican white woman from Mississippi who would never in a million years consider being in a crowd where Jesse Jackson might be haranguing her over a microphone. Now, bless Jesse Jackson — but if the crowd's going to stay a while, if the crowd's going to enjoy itself, if the feeling is going to be one of empowerment and then hope, my ergonomic suggestions make sense: chanting no more than 15 minutes out of an hour, and then having the great American reunion. The re-meeting, the beginning of the healing, the beginning of the post-Bush reconstruction. No alcohol, no weapons, no haranguing politicians, no amplifiers. Invite hundreds of little acoustic bands — Zydeco, New Orleans jazz — and emphasize that we need to meet one another again, we need a sense of community. We've been consciously divided [?] by decadent and evil men and women, and we can't just drift. We have been harmed, our country has been harmed, citizens have been killed, because government is out of anybody's control. So go forth and do you likewise. Oh, gorgeous little frog. Another frog. These little two-centimetre guys who are so hopeful that they're going to have kids next summer. Hopeful in a genetic, selfish-gene sense.

So, on Anasazi food: many of the dishes the Pueblo Indian women cook and serve today have been passed on from mother to daughter to great-granddaughter since Anasazi times. The one that is prepared most often is cornmeal mush, which the Indians call atole. This is made with one cup of coarsely ground white or yellow cornmeal, stirred into three cups of water and cooked slowly till it is thick and smooth. Some cooks put salt in the water when it starts to boil. Others add salt when the atole is about half done, till it tastes right, they say.

One stately plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and razor lay crossed. A yellow dressing-gown, ungirdled, was sustained gently behind him by the mild morning air. He held the bowl aloft and intoned, "Introibo ad altare Dei [?]." Halted, he peered down the dark winding stairs and called up coarsely, "Come up, Kinch! Come up, you fearful Jesuit!" Solemnly he came forward and mounted the round gunrest. He faced about and blessed gravely thrice the tower, the surrounding country, and the awakening mountains. Then, catching sight of Stephen Dedalus, he bent towards him and made rapid crosses in the air, gurgling in his throat and shaking his head. Stephen Dedalus, displeased and sleepy, leaned his arms on the top of the staircase, and looked coldly at the shaking, gurgling face that blessed him, equine in its length, and at the light untonsured hair, grained and hued like pale oak. Buck Mulligan peeped an instant under the mirror, and then covered the bowl smartly. "Back to barracks," he said sternly. He added, in a preacher's tone, "For this, oh, dearly beloved, is the genuine Christine, body and soul and blood and ouns. Slow music, please. Shut your eyes, gents. One moment. A little trouble about those white corpuscles. Silence, all." He peered sideways, up, and gave a long, low whistle of call, then paused a while in rapt attention, his even white teeth glistening here and there with gold points. Chrysostomos. Two strong shrill whistles answered through the calm. "Thanks, old chap," he cried briskly. "That will do nicely. Switch off the current, will you?" He skipped off the gunrest and looked gravely at his watcher, gathering about his legs the loose folds of his gown. The plump, shadowed face and sullen oval jowl recalled a prelate, patron of arts in the Middle Ages. A pleasant smile broke quietly over his lips. "The mockery of it," he said gaily. "Your absurd name, an ancient Greek." He pointed his finger in friendly jest and went over to the parapet, laughing to himself. Stephen Dedalus stepped up, following him wearily half-way, and sat down on the edge of the gunrest, watching him still as he propped his mirror on the parapet, dipped the brush in the bowl and lathered cheeks and neck. Buck Mulligan's gay voice went on. "My name is absurd too, Malachi Mulligan, two dactyls, but it has a Hellenic ring, hasn't it, tripping and sunny like the buck himself. We must go to Athens. Will you come, if I can get the aunt to fork out twenty quid?" He laid the brush aside, and, laughing with delight, cried, "Willy Crumb [?], come, the jejune Jesuit [?]." Ceasing, he began to shave with care. "Tell me, Mulligan," Stephen said quietly. "Yes, my love?" "How long is Haines going to stay in this tower?" Buck Mulligan showed a shaven cheek over his right shoulder. "God, isn't he dreadful?" he said frankly. "A ponderous Saxon. He thinks you're not a gentleman. God, these bloody English, bursting with money and indigestion. Because he comes from Oxford. You know, Dedalus, you have the real Oxford manner. He can't make you out. Oh, my name for you is the best. Kinch, the knife blade." He shaved warily over his chin. "He was raving all night about a black panther," Stephen said. "Where's his gun case?" "A woeful lunatic," Mulligan said. "Were you in a funk?" "I was," Stephen said, with energy and growing fear. "Out here in the dark with a man I don't know, raving and moaning to himself about shooting a black panther. You saved men from drowning. I'm not a hero, however. If he stays on here, I am off." Buck Mulligan frowned at the lather on his razor blade. He hopped down from his perch and began to search his trouser pockets hastily. "Scutter!" he cried thickly. He came over to the gunrest, and thrusting his hand into Stephen's upper pocket, said, "Lend us a loan of your nose-rag to wipe my razor." Stephen suffered him to pull out and hold up on show by its corner a dirty crumpled handkerchief. Buck Mulligan wiped the razor blade neatly. Then, gazing over the handkerchief, he said, "The bard's nose-rag. A new art colour for our Irish poets: snot-green. You can almost taste it, can't you?" He mounted to the parapet again and gazed out over Dublin Bay, his fair oak-pale hair stirring slightly. "God," he said quietly, "isn't the sea what Algy calls it, a great sweet mother? The snot-green sea, the scrotum-tightening sea. Epi oinopa ponton. Ah, Dedalus, the Greeks, I must teach you. You must read them in the original. Thalatta! Thalatta! She is our great, sweet mother. Come and look!" Stephen stood up and went over to the parapet. Leaning on it, he looked down on the water and on the mailboat, clearing the harbour mouth of Kingstown. "Our mighty mother," Buck Mulligan said. He turned abruptly his great searching eyes from the sea to Stephen's face. "The aunt thinks you killed your mother," he said. "That's why she won't let me have anything to do with you." "Someone killed her," Stephen said gloomily. "You could have knelt down, damn it, Kinch, when your dying mother asked you," Buck Mulligan said. "I'm hyperborean as much as you, but to think of your mother begging you with her last breath to kneel down and pray for her, and you refused. There's something sinister in you." He broke off and lathered again, lightly, his farther cheek. A tolerant smile curled his lips. "But a lovely mummer," he murmured to himself. "Kinch, the loveliest mummer of them all." He shaved evenly and with care, in silence, seriously. Stephen, an elbow rested on the jagged granite, leaned his palm against his brow, and gazed at the frayed edge of a shiny black coat sleeve. Pain, that was not yet the pain of love, fretted his heart. Silently, in a dream, she had come to him after her death, her wasted body within its loose brown grave clothes, giving off an odour of wax and rosewood, her breath that had bent upon him, mute, reproachful, a faint odour of wetted ashes. Across the threadbare cuffedge he saw the sea hailed as a great sweet mother by the well-fed voice beside him. The ring of bay and skyline held a dull green mass of liquid. A bowl of white china had stood beside her deathbed, holding the green sluggish bile, which she had torn up from her rotting liver by fits of loud groaning vomiting. Buck Mulligan wiped again his razor blade. "Ah, poor dogsbody," he said, in a kind voice. "I must give you a shirt and a few nose-rags. How are the second-hand breeks?" "They fit well enough," Stephen answered. Buck Mulligan attacked the hollow beneath his underlip. "The mockery of it," he said contentedly. "Second-leg they should be. God knows what poxy bowsy left them off. I have a lovely pair with a hair stripe, grey. You'll look spiffing in them. I'm not joking, Kinch. You look damn well when you're dressed." "Thanks," Stephen said. "I can't wear them if they are grey." "He can't wear them," Buck Mulligan told his face in the mirror. "Etiquette is etiquette. He kills his mother, but he can't wear grey trousers." He folded his razor neatly, and with stroking palps of fingers felt the smooth skin. Stephen turned his gaze from the sea into the plump face, with its smoke-blue, mobile eyes. "That fellow I was with in the Ship last night," said Buck Mulligan, "says you have G.P.I. "Facts can be similarly suppressed, so that at low energies one has what is known as an effective field theory in which these interactions are negligible.
